prompt: A colleague says the database password is safe because the Kubernetes Secret stores it in Base64. What is Base64?

choices.text: A light form of encryption, enough for internal use
choices.why: It has no key, so it is not encryption at any strength.

choices.text: An encoding that anybody reverses
choices.why: Right: base64 -d returned the password.

choices.text: A hash, so the password cannot be recovered
choices.why: Base64 decodes back exactly.

choices.text: Encryption with a key held by the cluster
choices.why: Encryption at rest is a separate cluster setting.

prompt: Why is HTTP Basic authentication acceptable only inside TLS?

choices.text: Because the Base64 in the header is too weak without TLS
choices.why: Base64 has no strength to be weak in.

choices.text: Because TLS hashes the password before it is sent
choices.why: TLS encrypts the whole request; it does not hash fields.

choices.text: The header is the password, merely encoded
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Because servers refuse Basic authentication on port 80
choices.why: Many do not; that is not why.

prompt: The third line of the side-by-side capture also looks like Base64. What separates it from the second?

choices.text: It is longer
choices.why: Length says nothing about secrecy.

choices.text: It ends in ==
choices.why: That is padding of the encoding.

choices.text: It uses a different alphabet
choices.why: Both use the Base64 alphabet.

choices.text: Reversing it also needs the key
choices.why: Right: underneath is AES ciphertext.

prompt: Base64 turns every 3 bytes into ___ characters.
How many keys did it take to recover the scheduler's "protected" password?
hint: Count the inputs of the two commands.

choices.text: None
choices.why: Right: Base64 and ROT13, both public rules.

choices.text: One, written in the vendor's manual
choices.why: The manual names the method; there is no key.

choices.text: Two, one per layer
choices.why: Neither layer has a key.

choices.text: The scheduler's licence key
choices.why: No licence was involved.

prompt: A vendor encrypts passwords in its configuration with AES, using a key compiled into the product. How should an auditor classify it?

choices.text: Encrypted at rest, compliant
choices.why: Every copy of the product holds the key.

choices.text: Plaintext password in configuration
choices.why: Right: obfuscation with better mathematics.

choices.text: Hashed, so unrecoverable
choices.why: AES is reversible with the key.

choices.text: Encoded, but safe while the file is private
choices.why: It is a finding whoever reads the file.

prompt: A mobile app hides an API key inside its compiled code with several layers of obfuscation. What should the team assume?
hint: Who has a copy of the app?

choices.text: The key is safe while the layers are not documented
choices.why: Undocumented is not secret; a decompiler reads it.

choices.text: The key is safe if it is also rotated yearly
choices.why: Rotation shortens exposure; it does not make it secret.

choices.text: The key is public, so limit its permissions
choices.why: Right: scope it server-side, as if published.

choices.text: Only rooted phones can extract it
choices.why: Any copy of the app can be decompiled.

prompt: Match each example to what it is.
hint: Apply the key question to each.

pairs.left: AES-GCM with a key in a secrets manager

prompt: The password is sealed with AES-GCM, and `aes-256.hex` is committed beside it in the same repository. What is it now?

choices.text: Encrypted, because AES-256-GCM is unbroken
choices.why: The cipher is fine; the key is beside the data.

choices.text: Obfuscation with better mathematics
choices.why: Right: whoever reads the repository reads the password.

choices.text: Encoded, since it is stored in Base64
choices.why: The Base64 is just how the bytes are written.

choices.text: Hashed, since GCM has a tag
choices.why: The tag is a MAC, not a password hash.

prompt: A vendor's document says customer data is "encrypted with SHA-256". What is the most useful response?

choices.text: Accept it: SHA-256 is a current algorithm
choices.why: Current, but it is a hash, not encryption.

choices.text: Ask them to use SHA-512 instead
choices.why: A bigger hash is still not encryption.

choices.text: Ask whether the data reads back, and with which key
choices.why: Right: if it reads back, it is not SHA-256; if not, it is not encryption.

choices.text: Conclude the data is unreadable by anybody
choices.why: Short or predictable values can be found by trying candidates.

prompt: Which statement about encoding, obfuscation and encryption is correct?
hint: The test is about the key, not the look.

choices.text: Ciphertext can be told from encoded data by looking at it
choices.why: Ciphertext is often written in Base64 too.

choices.text: Two layers of encoding are as strong as one of encryption
choices.why: Zero plus zero is zero.

choices.text: Encryption is as secret as the place its key is kept
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Obfuscation is fine for passwords if the method is proprietary
choices.why: Proprietary methods leak with every copy.

prompt: Order these from least to most protection for a stored database password.
hint: Who can recover it in each case?
items: AES with a key compiled into the product
AES-GCM with the key in a secrets manager

prompt: Which of these are encodings? Choose all that apply.
hint: No key, public rule, anybody reverses.

choices.text: PEM
choices.why: Yes: Base64 between marker lines.

choices.text: Hexadecimal
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: URL encoding (%20 for a space)
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: AES-GCM
choices.why: No: it needs a key.
